stem: What is AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) primarily used for?
options: Storing photos and videos in the cloud
Running virtual servers in multiple regions
Controlling who can do what in an AWS account — authentication and authorization
Monitoring website traffic in real time
explanation: IAM is AWS's identity service: it authenticates identities (users, roles, applications) and authorizes what API actions they may perform on which resources. Everything in AWS is denied by default until IAM grants it.
hint: Think: who is allowed to touch what? That is an identity question.
source: AWS Documentation — What is IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com)

stem: An IAM user is best described as:
options: A temporary token that expires after 12 hours
An identity representing a person or application with long-term credentials
A billing report for an AWS account
The physical server that hosts your application
explanation: An IAM user is a persistent identity inside your account — it can have a console password and/or access keys. Use IAM users for people (or workloads) that need long-term credentials, and roles for everything else.
hint: Users are long-term. What kind of identity sticks around for months?
source: AWS Documentation — What is IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com)

stem: Why does AWS recommend NOT using the root user for everyday tasks?
options: The root user cannot access the AWS Management Console
The root user has unrestricted access to the account, so a compromise is catastrophic
The root user is charged extra per API call
The root user cannot be given MFA
explanation: The root user can do anything in the account — its permissions cannot be limited by design. AWS best practice: lock it away (MFA on, no access keys) and do daily work with an IAM administrative user instead.
hint: What makes the root user special — and dangerous?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Root user best practices (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)

stem: Which is the FIRST thing AWS recommends after creating a new account?
options: Launch an EC2 instance to test the account
Share the root password with the team
Delete all default IAM policies
Enable MFA on the root user and create an IAM administrative user
explanation: AWS's administrator best-practices checklist starts with: sign in as root, enable MFA, create an administrative user in IAM, then safeguard the root credentials and never use them for everyday tasks.
hint: Before doing anything else — how do you secure the most powerful identity?
source: AWS Sign-In User Guide — Security best practices for AWS account administrators (docs.aws.amazon.com/signin/latest/userguide/best-practices-admin.html)

stem: An IAM group is:
options: A billing consolidation of multiple AWS accounts
A temporary credential issued by AWS STS
A collection of IAM users that share the same attached policies
A set of EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone
explanation: Groups let you attach a policy once and have every member user inherit it. Best practice: put users in groups and attach policies to the group, not to individual users — far easier to manage as the team grows.
hint: Groups bundle people so you manage permissions once, not per person.
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

stem: AWS best practice for assigning permissions is to attach policies to:
options: Groups and roles rather than individual users
EC2 security groups
Individual IAM users, one by one
The root user only
explanation: Attaching policies to groups and roles (not individual users) reduces the chance that an identity keeps excessive privileges as people change teams. AWS Config even has a managed rule (iam-user-no-policies-check) enforcing this.
hint: People change jobs; groups describe jobs. Where should the policy live?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

stem: How does an IAM role differ from an IAM user?
options: A role has no long-term credentials; it issues temporary credentials when assumed
Users are free but roles cost money per assumption
Roles can only be used in a single AWS Region
Roles are for humans, users are for applications
explanation: Roles have no passwords or access keys of their own. A trusted principal (user, service, or account) assumes the role via STS and gets temporary credentials that expire automatically — far safer than long-lived keys.
hint: Which identity is designed to hand out credentials that expire?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — IAM roles (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html)

stem: An application running on an EC2 instance needs to read files from an S3 bucket. The most secure approach is to:
options: Make the S3 bucket public
Attach an IAM role to the EC2 instance (instance profile)
Email the root user's credentials to the developer
Embed an IAM user's access keys in the application code
explanation: Attaching a role to the instance lets AWS inject temporary, automatically rotated credentials into the instance. No long-lived keys to leak, rotate, or accidentally commit to Git.
hint: Where should credentials live so nobody has to store them?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — IAM roles (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html)

stem: An IAM policy is:
options: A physical contract signed with AWS
A JSON document that defines Allow or Deny permissions for actions on resources
An invoice for IAM usage
A network firewall rule for a VPC
explanation: Policies are JSON documents with statements containing Effect (Allow/Deny), Action (API calls), and Resource (ARNs). They attach to users, groups, or roles to define what is permitted.
hint: IAM speaks JSON. What does that JSON describe?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Policies and permissions (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html)

stem: In a policy statement, the 'Effect' element can be:
options: True or False
Allow or Deny
Read or Write
Public or Private
explanation: Every policy statement has an Effect of Allow or Deny. Evaluation: an explicit Deny anywhere always wins; an Allow grants the action; with no Allow anywhere, the request is implicitly denied.
hint: Two words decide everything in a statement. Which two?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Policies and permissions (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html)

stem: A user has one policy allowing s3:GetObject on a bucket and another policy explicitly denying s3:GetObject on the same bucket. The result is:
options: Allowed, because two policies beat one
Denied — an explicit deny always overrides any allow
Allowed, because Allow was written first
Allowed only on weekends
explanation: Explicit deny is a veto: it overrides every allow, no matter where the allow lives. The golden rule of IAM evaluation is Deny > Allow > implicit deny.
hint: When Allow and Deny collide, which one is the veto?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — IAM policy evaluation logic (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html)

stem: An IAM user with NO policies attached tries to list S3 buckets. What happens?
options: The user is automatically given AdministratorAccess
The request is allowed because S3 is a public service
The request is allowed for 24 hours, then denied
The request is denied — by default, everything is implicitly denied
explanation: AWS starts from implicit deny: with no policy granting an action, the request fails. Permissions must be explicitly granted — the root user is the only exception.
hint: No policy attached. Does AWS default to yes or no?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — IAM policy evaluation logic (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html)

stem: Which policy type is maintained by AWS and updated automatically when AWS adds new services?
options: Inline policy
Customer inline policy
Bucket ACL
AWS managed policy
explanation: AWS managed policies (e.g. AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess) are created and maintained by AWS, so they stay current as services evolve. Customer managed policies are yours to maintain; inline policies are embedded in a single identity.
hint: Who keeps the policy up to date — you or AWS?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Policies and permissions (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html)

stem: An inline policy differs from a managed policy in that it:
options: Is automatically updated by AWS
Can be attached to multiple accounts at once
Is embedded directly in a single user, group, or role and cannot be reused
Never needs a JSON document
explanation: Inline policies live inside exactly one identity — delete the identity and the policy goes with it. Managed policies (AWS or customer) are standalone and reusable across many identities.
hint: Which policy type is glued to one identity and dies with it?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Policies and permissions (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html)

stem: A policy attached to an S3 bucket (a bucket policy) is an example of a:
options: Session policy
Identity-based policy
Resource-based policy
Password policy
explanation: Resource-based policies attach to the resource itself and say who may access it. Identity-based policies attach to users/groups/roles and say what they may do. S3 bucket policies are the classic resource-based example.
hint: Is the policy stuck to the person or to the thing?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Policies and permissions (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html)

stem: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) improves security because:
options: It encrypts all S3 data by default
It makes passwords longer automatically
It replaces IAM users with roles
It requires a second factor (something you have) in addition to the password
explanation: MFA adds 'something you have' — a virtual authenticator app, hardware token, or security key — on top of 'something you know' (the password). Even a stolen password alone is not enough.
hint: Password = something you know. What does MFA add?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Multi-factor authentication (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html)

stem: For which identity does AWS MOST strongly recommend enabling MFA?
options: The AWS account root user
A service-linked role
An IAM group
An IAM user with read-only S3 access
explanation: The root user is the single most powerful identity in the account. AWS best practice: enable MFA on root first, then on all human users — especially privileged ones.
hint: Which identity could do the most damage if compromised?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Multi-factor authentication (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html)

stem: Which of these is a valid MFA device type in AWS?
options: A fingerprint stored in the IAM console
A virtual MFA app on a phone, a hardware TOTP token, or a FIDO2 security key
A CAPTCHA puzzle on the sign-in page
An SMS sent to any phone number worldwide
explanation: AWS supports virtual MFA applications (e.g. authenticator apps), hardware TOTP tokens, and FIDO2/passkey security keys. Choose the device type that fits your recovery plan.
hint: AWS lists three families of MFA devices. Which option names them?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Multi-factor authentication (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html)

stem: The principle of least privilege means:
options: Requiring MFA for every single API call
Deleting all IAM users every 90 days
Granting only the minimum permissions needed to do the job, nothing more
Giving every user AdministratorAccess so nothing ever breaks
explanation: Least privilege: start with the smallest set of permissions that lets the work happen, and add more only when needed. If a key leaks, minimal permissions limit the blast radius.
hint: If a leaked key had admin access, an attacker could spin up expensive servers in minutes. How do you limit that damage?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

stem: A developer only needs to read objects from one S3 bucket. The least-privilege policy is:
options: s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::that-bucket/*
AdministratorAccess on *
iam:* on *
s3:* on *
explanation: Least privilege matches the action (GetObject, not s3:*) to the exact resource (that bucket, not *). Broad wildcards are the opposite of least privilege.
hint: Match the permission to the exact job: read, one bucket.
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

stem: An IAM password policy is used to:
options: Encrypt the root user's email address
Prevent users from ever changing their passwords
Set requirements like minimum length and complexity for IAM user passwords
Automatically rotate access keys every day
explanation: A password policy enforces length, complexity, and rotation rules for IAM user passwords. Note it does not apply to the root user — another reason to protect root separately.
hint: Where do rules like 'minimum 14 characters' live in IAM?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

stem: Programmatic access to AWS (CLI/SDK) uses which credential pair?
options: MFA serial and token
Account ID and region code
Username and PIN
Access key ID and secret access key
explanation: The CLI and SDKs authenticate with an access key ID (like a username) and secret access key (like a password). Guard the secret — anyone holding both can act as that identity.
hint: Console uses password + MFA. What does the CLI use?
source: AWS Documentation — What is IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com)

stem: Which of the following is an IAM security best practice?
options: Rotating credentials regularly and never sharing them
Using the root user for daily development work
Sharing one IAM user among the whole team to save effort
Committing access keys to a Git repository for backup
explanation: AWS best practices: one identity per human, rotate credentials regularly, never share or commit secrets, use roles instead of long-term keys, and keep root locked away.
hint: Three of these are horror stories. Which one is the good habit?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

stem: A company has two AWS accounts and wants developers in Account A to read a bucket in Account B. The standard approach is:
options: Share Account B's root password with the developers
Make the bucket public
Copy the bucket to Account A every night
Create a role in Account B that Account A users can assume (cross-account role)
explanation: Cross-account roles are the designed solution: Account B's role trusts Account A's principals, and developers assume it via STS for temporary credentials. No shared passwords, no public buckets.
hint: Two accounts, one bucket. What trusts what?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — IAM roles (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html)

stem: A trust policy on an IAM role defines:
options: Who is allowed to assume the role
The password policy for the role
Which API actions the role is allowed to perform
How much the role costs per month
explanation: Every role has two policy types: the trust policy (who can assume it — users, services, or other accounts) and the permissions policy (what the role can do once assumed).
hint: One policy says WHO can wear the hat; the other says WHAT the hat can do. Which is the trust policy?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — IAM roles (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html)

stem: IAM users, groups, roles, and policies are:
options: Zonal — tied to a single Availability Zone
Global — they apply across all Regions in the account
Regional — you must recreate them in every Region
Billed per Region they are used in
explanation: IAM is a global service: identities and policies exist once per account and work in every Region. (Service-specific endpoints still apply, but the identity itself is global.)
hint: Do you create your IAM users once, or once per Region?
source: AWS Documentation — What is IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com)

stem: An IAM user can be a member of:
options: No groups — groups are only for roles
Exactly one group, chosen at account creation
Up to one group per Region
Multiple groups at the same time
explanation: A user can belong to many groups and inherits the union of their policies. Design groups around job functions (e.g. Developers, Auditors) and place people accordingly.
hint: Can one person wear two job-function hats?
source: AWS Documentation — What is IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com)

stem: The IAM credential report helps administrators to:
options: See who has MFA enabled and whose access keys are old, across the account
Translate policies into other languages
Generate monthly invoices
Delete S3 buckets automatically
explanation: The credential report is an account-wide snapshot: MFA status, password age, access-key age and last use per user. Pair it with IAM Access Advisor (per-user service usage) to trim unused permissions.
hint: One report, whole account: who has MFA, whose keys are stale?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Security best practices in IAM (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)

stem: Which task can ONLY be performed by the AWS account root user?
options: Closing the AWS account
Starting an EC2 instance
Creating an IAM user
Reading an S3 object
explanation: A small set of tasks is root-only — closing the account is the classic example (along with changing the support plan in some cases). Everything else should be done with IAM identities.
hint: Most things IAM admins can do. What's reserved for the account owner alone?
source: AWS IAM User Guide — Root user best practices (docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)

stem: A new team member needs console access to manage EC2 instances. Following best practices, you should:
options: Email them an access key pair with AdministratorAccess
Share the root user credentials with them
Create an IAM user, add them to the EC2-operators group, enable MFA
Give them the account ID and let them figure it out
explanation: Best-practice onboarding: one IAM user per human, permissions via a group (not attached directly), MFA enabled, least-privilege policies. No shared credentials, no root usage.
hint: One person, one identity, permissions through a group, MFA on. Which option does all of that?
source: AWS Sign-In User Guide — Security best practices for AWS account administrators (docs.aws.amazon.com/signin/latest/userguide/best-practices-admin.html)
